historical_timeline.summary: Atrial fibrillation while running; admitted to hospital; ECG and cardiac ultrasound otherwise normal.
Sinus rhythm restored on medication; discharged.
Diagnosed with Graves' disease later the same week.
Radioactive iodine for Graves' disease; weight loss partly regained; thyroid hormone level later low, and thyroid hormone replacement begun.
Physical examination: thyroid function normal on Synthroid 0.15 mg a day; normal ECG.

claims.statement: George Herbert Walker Bush was born in Milton, Massachusetts, on June 12, 1924.

On May 4, 1991, he developed atrial fibrillation while running at Camp David; it presented as unusual fatigue during the run. He was flown to Bethesda Naval Hospital, where an electrocardiogram showed no abnormality except the irregular rhythm and a cardiac ultrasound showed no structural abnormality and normal heart function. Treatment began with digoxin.
claims.clinical_interpretation: White House statement issued the same evening.

claims.statement: On May 5, 1991, the White House said he still had atrial fibrillation, with no sign of heart damage or heart attack, and that procainamide had been added to digoxin; electrical cardioversion would be considered if the rhythm did not return to normal.

His normal rhythm returned late on May 5, atrial fibrillation recurred early on May 6, and cardioversion was judged unnecessary because his response to medication was encouraging. He was discharged on May 6 and was in normal sinus rhythm later that day, on digoxin and procainamide.
Later in the same week he was diagnosed with Graves' disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Editorial note to the May 4 statement in the Public Papers.

claims.statement: A physician's account published in 2016 reports a ventricular rate of 150 beats per minute on arrival at the hospital, an overactive thyroid as the explanation for the atrial fibrillation, treatment with an oral dose of radioactive iodine, a thyroid hormone level that became too low within a few months, and synthetic thyroid hormone thereafter for life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Secondary account by a physician writing for a newspaper; the exact date of the radioactive iodine treatment was not verified.

claims.statement: Newsweek reported that he had regained eight of the 13 pounds he lost after doctors used radioactive iodine to control his overactive thyroid.
claims.clinical_interpretation: News report; the article date was not verified.

claims.statement: After his physical examination on March 26, 1992, the White House reported that his thyroid function remained completely normal on Synthroid 0.15 milligrams a day, that his electrocardiogram was normal and there was no evidence of heart disease, that hip and neck x-rays showed mild degenerative osteoarthritis, and that raised pressure in his left eye was stable without signs of glaucoma.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Confirms lifelong levothyroxine replacement and sinus rhythm after treatment. Later than the episode; recorded in the claims only.

claims.statement: He died on November 30, 2018, at the age of 94.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Manage new paroxysmal atrial fibrillation triggered by Graves' hyperthyroidism in a fit 66-year-old: rate control with a beta-blocker and no cardioversion or antiarrhythmic while thyrotoxic, CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scoring with a shared anticoagulation decision, methimazole pretreatment with safety monitoring, radioactive iodine as definitive treatment, recognition of the expected hypothyroidism afterwards, levothyroxine started at a cautious dose and titrated by TSH, confirmation of sustained sinus rhythm before stopping anticoagulation, on the CMID atrial fibrillation and hypothyroidism schedules with the 1988 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS and ATA guidelines.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Bush returns twelve days after starting methimazole 20 mg daily, on metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and apixaban 5 mg twice daily since his hospital stay. He has had no palpitations or irregular pulse on his home monitor and feels well. He has walked daily but has not run yet, as advised. He has had no fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, rash, itching, yellow eyes, or dark urine on methimazole, and no bleeding or bruising on apixaban. He takes every dose. He has no eye pain, grittiness, or double vision. He saw the endocrinologist this morning, and radioactive iodine is planned for next week.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Bush returns seven weeks after radioactive iodine. He stopped methimazole three days before the treatment and has not restarted it. For about two weeks he has felt more tired in the afternoons, a little cold in air-conditioned rooms, and slightly constipated, and he has regained 2.2 kg. He has had no palpitations, and his home pulse checks have been regular. He takes metoprolol and apixaban every day, with no bleeding. He has started running again, two miles three days a week, without symptoms. He has no neck pain, eye symptoms, or swallowing trouble. He knows of no snoring and has no daytime sleepiness.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Bush is a 67-year-old man who returns for his subsequent annual wellness visit five weeks after his four-month review. He had his initial annual wellness visit with his previous primary care clinician last year. Since the spring he has had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation triggered by Graves' disease, treated with radioactive iodine, and is now on levothyroxine for the hypothyroidism that followed. He completed the health risk assessment before the visit. He takes levothyroxine 100 mcg each morning before breakfast, five weeks after the dose was raised, and has missed no doses. Metoprolol and apixaban were stopped at the last visit after a 14-day monitor showed sinus rhythm throughout; he has had no palpitations, lightheadedness, or breathlessness since. He runs three miles four days a week. He has no new concerns.

referral.question: New paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in a fit 66-year-old, with thyroid tests showing hyperthyroidism and a positive TSH receptor antibody. Please confirm Graves' disease, assess the eyes, and advise on definitive treatment and on the thyroid course afterwards
referral.pertinent_history: Atrial fibrillation began four days ago as unusual tiredness while running, with a fast ventricular rate on arrival at hospital. ECG showed no abnormality apart from the rhythm, and the echocardiogram was normal. Sinus rhythm returned on medication without cardioversion, with one brief recurrence before discharge. Discharged on metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and apixaban 5 mg twice daily (CHA2DS2-VASc 1, HAS-BLED 1, shared decision). Today: sinus rhythm at 88; TSH 0.005 mIU/L, free T4 3.6 ng/dL, total T3 280 ng/dL, TSH receptor antibody 8.2 IU/L; white cell count 6.8 and neutrophils 3.9 x10³/µL; ALT 32 U/L; creatinine 0.92 mg/dL. Diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid; no eye signs. Never used tobacco. Methimazole 20 mg daily started today
questions: Do you agree this is Graves' disease, or is an uptake scan needed to exclude a nodular goiter or thyroiditis?
Which definitive treatment do you advise (radioactive iodine, long-term methimazole, or surgery), given his age and atrial fibrillation?
How should methimazole and the beta-blocker be handled before and after treatment?
Is there any Graves' orbitopathy, and does he need steroid cover?
What thyroid course should we expect afterwards, and when should levothyroxine start?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Bush is seen at the request of Dr. Whitford, twelve days after starting methimazole 20 mg daily. Before the atrial fibrillation he had noticed more tiredness on his runs, and some weight loss despite a good appetite. He feels better on methimazole and metoprolol. He has had no neck pain, recent viral illness, iodine contrast, or amiodarone, and no eye pain, grittiness, bulging, or double vision. He has had no methimazole side effects. He has never used tobacco. He wants a treatment that settles the problem quickly so he can get back to running and a full schedule
consultant_note.data_reviewed: The hospital ECG and echocardiogram, the intake thyroid tests and TSH receptor antibody, the baseline blood count and liver and kidney tests, and today's free T4, total T3, TSH, neutrophil count, and ALT

exam.finding: Well and calm
No lid retraction, lid lag, proptosis, chemosis, or redness; eye movements full; clinical activity score 0
Diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid without nodules; no bruit
Regular rhythm at 72 per minute
Fine tremor of the outstretched hands

assessment.assessment: Confirmed: suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and total T3, a positive TSH receptor antibody, and a diffuse goiter. No uptake scan is needed. Responding to methimazole: free T4 2.2 ng/dL, total T3 176 ng/dL. Neutrophils and ALT are normal
None (clinical activity score 0). As a never smoker without eye disease, his risk of new or worse eye disease after radioactive iodine is low, and steroid cover is not needed
In sinus rhythm on metoprolol. Most thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation does not recur once thyroid levels are controlled, which favors prompt definitive treatment

recommendations: Radioactive iodine as definitive treatment: it is effective, quick, and avoids long-term antithyroid drug risks. Long-term methimazole is less suitable because relapse after stopping is common, and surgery is not needed without a large goiter, compressive symptoms, or eye disease. Iodine-131, 15 mCi, booked for next week
Stop methimazole three days before treatment; restarting it afterwards is not needed while free T4 is only mildly raised and he is on a beta-blocker
Continue metoprolol until he is no longer thyrotoxic, then taper
No steroid cover; report any eye symptoms promptly
Free T4 and total T3 within one to two months of treatment, then every four to six weeks until stable

Hypothyroidism is expected within two to three months. Start levothyroxine once free T4 falls below normal, at a dose below full replacement because of his age and recent atrial fibrillation, and titrate by TSH every four to eight weeks to 0.4 to 4.0 mIU/L
Reassess anticoagulation once he is no longer thyrotoxic and sinus rhythm has been confirmed on ambulatory monitoring
Written radiation-safety instructions for the first week after treatment

consultant_note.follow_up: Endocrinology will give the radioactive iodine next week. Primary care will monitor thyroid levels and levothyroxine dosing on the CMID hypothyroidism schedule. Endocrinology will see him again for eye symptoms, persistent hyperthyroidism at six months, or difficulty reaching the TSH target
